title: Imperfect-by-contract DRAM tier for noise-trained AI weights
idea: Inverts 'memory must be perfect': a DRAM tier runs with refresh stretched 8x (~512 ms) and a published raw BER (1e-7 to 1e-5); training frameworks inject bit-flip noise matched to that datasheet BER in the final epochs so models are certified robust, and the runtime places weights and KV-cache only on this tier.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3) cut ~85% on the tier; dies failing standard retention bins become sellable, raising effective supply ~10-15%.

title: Exponent bits in strong rows, mantissa LSBs in weak rows
idea: Inverts 'all bits are equally important': rows are ranked by retention at test; the controller's address swizzle uses the fused ranking so sign/exponent bytes of BF16/FP8 words land in top-retention rows and low mantissa bits in the weakest rows, which are refreshed 4-8x less often.
why: The retention tail (fact 3) no longer sets the refresh rate for most bits; ~50-70% refresh energy cut with <0.1% accuracy loss on weights.

title: Known weak cells decoded as erasures, halving ECC parity
idea: Inverts 'errors are random and unknown': the weak-cell map from test and in-field scrub is held by the controller and fed to a Reed-Solomon decoder as erasure locations; RS corrects two erasures per unknown error, so the same parity tolerates twice the weak cells, or the same cells with half the parity.
why: Refresh can be set by the 1e-6 instead of the 1e-9 retention quantile (~4x longer interval), or ECC overhead drops from 12.5% to ~6%.

title: Write data so weak cells hold their leak-to value
idea: Inverts 'data is stored as-is': each 64-bit word carries 2 coset bits selecting one of four XOR masks; the write encoder picks the mask that leaves the word's known weak cells (true-cells leak to 0, anti-cells to 1) already in their discharged state, so leakage cannot corrupt them.
why: Neutralizes most retention-tail cells (fact 3) for 3% overhead; with 1-2 weak cells per word the refresh interval can rise ~4-8x.

title: Open-bitline twin-cell mode for hot and weak rows
idea: Inverts 'one bit, one cell, single-ended read': in open-bitline arrays the controller switches a row pair (row i in mat A and the mirror row in mat B, which share sense amps) into differential mode, writing true and complement and activating both, so the sense amp sees ~2x signal and common-mode disturbance (hammer, coupling, VARY noise) cancels.
why: Hammered or weak rows survive ~10x more activations and ~4x longer retention, costing half capacity only in those rows (<2% of the die).

title: Garbage collector evacuates objects off error-rising rows
idea: Inverts 'errors are hidden from software': the controller exports per-row correctable-error counters to managed runtimes (JVM, Go, Python); their copying garbage collector, which already moves objects, preferentially evacuates live objects from rows with rising syndromes and marks those frames cold-only.
why: Zero-cost migration makes dies with growing faults (VRT, aging) usable; turns ~1% faulty rows into non-events instead of DIMM replacements.

title: Deliberately short capacitors, rescued by two-level ECC
idea: Inverts 'every cell must meet retention on its own': cut capacitor aspect ratio from ~70:1 to ~45:1 (Cs ~3 fF), halving deep-etch and ALD time, and accept a fat retention tail handled by on-die BCH (t=2 per 256b) plus controller chipkill at a modestly faster refresh.
why: Sidesteps the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and capital (fact 4): ~15-25% lower array process cost and higher pillar yield for ~8% extra parity.

title: Elastic parity that grows as the chip ages
idea: Inverts 'ECC strength is fixed at design time': pages start with a light code (CRC+SEC); when a page's syndrome rate rises the controller allocates extra parity from a pooled spare region and re-encodes it with a stronger LDPC, spending protection only where wear and tail cells appear.
why: Average ECC overhead ~3% instead of 12.5% while weak or aged regions get >4x stronger protection; extends module service life.

title: Wordlines as on-die heaters that anneal retention traps
idea: Inverts 'a leaky cell is permanently leaky': during idle, a driver mode passes current end-to-end through segmented wordline metal to Joule-heat one mat to ~200-300 C for milliseconds, annealing the interface and bulk traps behind VRT and GIDL tail cells.
why: Periodic self-healing of the leakage tail (fact 3) could recover 2-4x retention on aged parts and may reset hammer-induced trap damage.

title: Chaos-engineering controller that probes margins with shadow writes
idea: Inverts 'operate safely inside a fixed guardband': the controller continuously writes shadow copies of live lines into a scratch row using aggressive timings and refresh, compares them with the protected original, and learns per-bank safe tRCD/tRAS/refresh envelopes that track temperature and aging.
why: Recovers the 20-40% timing and refresh guardband sized for worst-case cells (facts 3, 10), raising usable bandwidth and lowering energy.

title: Bounded-error number encoding makes bit flips harmless
idea: Inverts 'binary place-value storage': KV-cache and activations are stored in a code where any single flipped cell moves the value by at most one quantization step (split-unary or Gray-coded mantissa, exponent stored twice), so errors become tiny noise instead of exponent blowups.
why: Removes ECC need for >50% of AI memory traffic and tolerates ~10x higher raw BER, enabling refresh-starved or weaker cells.

title: Store the recipe, not the parity: lineage recompute on error
idea: Inverts 'memory must correct its own errors': for recomputable tensors (activations, decompressed weights, caches) the runtime replaces SECDED with a 4-bit detection CRC plus a pointer to the producing kernel; on a detected error it recomputes only the affected tile from its inputs.
why: Halves ECC overhead for recomputable data and tolerates ~100x higher BER, permitting much longer refresh; recompute cost is negligible at realistic error rates.

title: Dual-threshold sense amps feed soft-decision LDPC
idea: Inverts 'a DRAM read is a hard 0/1 decision': each sense amp gets a second offset comparator that flags weak-0/weak-1 when bitline signal is near the reference, giving NAND-style soft information; a soft-decision LDPC uses it to correct ~2x more errors per parity bit.
why: Cells can run with 30-40% less signal margin (smaller Cs, longer refresh; facts 1, 3) for a small periphery cost.

title: Mat parity row catches whole-row hammer bursts
idea: Inverts 'each word is corrected independently': every 512-row subarray dedicates one row to the XOR of all its rows, kept current on writes by in-array XOR; a row wiped by a hammer burst or wordline fault is rebuilt from the parity row and its siblings.
why: Converts row-hammer bursts (fact 9) and wordline failures from uncorrectable to correctable at ~0.2% capacity overhead.

title: Refresh that shifts every row one slot, dissolving neighbors
idea: Inverts 'a row's physical neighbors are fixed': each refresh pass copies row i into row i+1 with in-subarray copy instead of restoring in place, then bumps a per-subarray offset register, so logical rows migrate continuously and no aggressor stays beside the same victim for more than one window.
why: Defeats targeted row hammer (fact 9) and spreads disturb at near-zero cost, since refresh already reads and rewrites every row.

title: Buy untested die by the kilogram, grade them in-system
idea: Inverts 'the vendor tests and bins every die': hyperscalers buy dies with only gross-function test, skipping hours of retention and speed test, at a discount; servers run a self-test boot phase, build each die's weak-cell map and place data by quality tier.
why: Test is ~10-15% of DRAM cost and binning discards marginal die; raises usable supply 5-10% and lowers cost per bit.

title: Completion-detecting sense amps: weak cells read slow, not wrong
idea: Inverts 'memory timing is synchronous and fixed': each sense-amp group asserts a done signal once its latch resolves past a full-rail threshold; the bank uses this asynchronous handshake, so a low-charge weak cell simply takes 2-3 ns longer instead of being mis-sensed at a fixed tRCD.
why: Turns the charge/retention tail (facts 1, 3) from an error source into a small latency tail; strong cells finish ~15% faster than the worst-case timing.

title: Park bitlines at the data's safe rail during standby
idea: Inverts 'bitlines idle at VDD/2': in self-refresh, columns whose mapped weak cells hold 1 are parked at VDD and others at ground, so residual subthreshold leakage through off access transistors flows toward the stored value instead of away from it.
why: Removes the subthreshold share of the retention tail for mapped weak cells; ~2x longer self-refresh interval, 10-15% idle power saved.

title: Constrained codes that never write the worst coupling pattern
idea: Inverts 'any data pattern must be storable': a 64b/66b-style constrained code forbids the stripe and checkerboard patterns that maximize bitline-to-bitline and cell-to-cell coupling, so the array only ever stores mild patterns.
why: Data-pattern-dependent failures, a large share of the retention and hammer tail, drop ~3-10x for 3% capacity.

title: Matrix checksums replace DRAM ECC for AI weights
idea: Inverts 'memory must protect itself': weight matrices carry row and column checksum vectors (algorithm-based fault tolerance); the GEMM kernel verifies output checksums and corrects single weight-tile errors, so HBM holding weights runs without on-die ECC or with relaxed refresh.
why: Reclaims the ~12% ECC area and bandwidth in HBM (fact 6) and tolerates higher raw BER for <2% compute overhead.

title: Triple-row activation gives free analog majority voting
idea: Inverts 'only one row opens at a time': critical data (page tables, kernel, model metadata) is written into three rows of one subarray; a read opens all three at once so charge sharing makes the sense amp resolve the majority, giving TMR voting in a single access with no logic.
why: Hammer- and retention-proof storage (facts 3, 9) for the ~1% of data whose corruption is catastrophic, with no added latency.

title: RAID-5 across HBM stacks accepts one dead die
idea: Inverts 'every die in a stack must work': the accelerator controller stripes each line across 8 HBM stacks with one parity channel, so a stack with one failed core die or channel ships and runs degraded instead of being scrapped.
why: HBM stacked-yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) could fall by more than half; parity costs ~12% capacity but saves whole stacks.

title: Analog leaky-bucket capacitor physically caps row activations
idea: Inverts 'hammer defense needs digital counters': each wordline-driver group gets a small capacitor that every activation drains by a fixed packet while a resistor slowly refills it; below threshold the driver triggers neighbor refresh or refuses further ACTs until it recovers.
why: Row-hammer protection (fact 9) at ~1k-ACT thresholds without SRAM tracker tables, ~0.5% area versus multi-percent for trackers.

title: One block implant makes the access transistor asymmetric
idea: Inverts 'access transistors are symmetric': the single added mask blocks the bitline side so a low-dose counter-doping implant grades only the storage-node junction, lowering the peak field that drives GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling where the leakage tail originates.
why: Tail leakage 3-10x lower (fact 3) for ~4x longer refresh, cutting refresh's 16-33% idle power with one non-EUV implant mask.

title: Recombination barrier implant stops hammer electrons between wordlines
idea: Inverts 'the substrate is a passive bystander': one implant mask places a deep p+ or carbon-rich trap layer between adjacent buried wordlines so electrons injected from the aggressor channel recombine before reaching the victim storage node.
why: Raises the row-hammer threshold (fact 9) from ~1k to ~10k+ activations, shrinking mitigation SRAM and extra refresh; one implant mask.

title: Odd and even buried wordlines at different depths
idea: Inverts 'all wordlines sit at the same depth': the single added mask covers even rows during an extra recess etch so odd buried wordlines sit ~15-20 nm deeper, staggering aggressor gates vertically away from neighbor storage-node junctions without changing pitch.
why: Weakens passing-gate and neighbor coupling, the dominant hammer paths at F~12 nm (fact 9); estimated 3-5x higher hammer threshold.

title: Split wells so idle mats get local back-bias
idea: Inverts 'body bias is one global setting': one mask segments the array's deep well per mat, so in self-refresh the controller applies stronger negative back-bias only to mats holding mapped weak cells while active mats keep fast bias.
why: Cuts subthreshold leakage in weak mats ~10x during idle (fact 3) without slowing active access; ~2x self-refresh interval.

title: One mask grows deliberately weak sentinel cells that call refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh runs on a timer': the single added mask partially blocks the mold etch for a few sentinel cells per subarray so their capacitors are shorter and fail first; a sentinel flip, found by a cheap probe read, triggers refresh of only that subarray.
why: Refresh follows actual local temperature and leakage instead of worst-case 32/64 ms timers; ~50-75% refresh cut (fact 3).

title: Cut the cell plate into strips and bump it on reads
idea: Inverts 'the cell plate is a passive common electrode': one mask cuts the plate into row-group strips; when a row with known weak cells is read, its strip is pulsed +0.2-0.3 V just before sensing so capacitive coupling lifts the storage node and the bitline signal.
why: ~30% more sense signal for weak cells (facts 1, 3), so smaller Cs or longer refresh becomes tolerable; one non-critical mask.

title: Maskless per-die repair layer written after test
idea: Inverts 'every die gets identical masks': the one added litho step is maskless direct-write (e-beam or laser), personalized per die from its wafer-test map, writing a few hundred repair links that reroute weak rows and columns to spares far beyond fuse-bank capacity.
why: Repair is no longer capped by fuse area in the periphery (fact 7); a few % yield and much heavier weak-tail tolerance, with no physical mask to buy.

title: Deuterium chimneys through the nitride over the array
idea: Inverts 'barrier layers must seal everything': the single added mask opens small windows in the hydrogen-blocking nitride over the array so a final deuterium anneal reaches storage-node junctions and gate interfaces, passivating dangling bonds with harder-to-break Si-D bonds.
why: Shrinks the trap-driven VRT and retention tail (fact 3) ~2-3x and hardens cells against hammer-induced trap generation; one non-EUV mask.

title: Engineered damage sites that getter metals away from cells
idea: Inverts 'defects are always bad': one mask defines implant-damage gettering zones at mat boundaries that pull Fe, Cu and Ni contaminants during later anneals away from storage-node junctions, where they would form generation centers.
why: Lowers the contaminant-driven retention tail (fact 3) and relaxes purity specs on chemicals and crucibles (resource chokepoints) at constant refresh.

title: Thermal moat isolates the cool array from hot periphery
idea: Inverts 'the whole die shares one temperature': a single mask etches an air-gapped ring trench between the array and the hot periphery and I/O, forcing periphery heat to flow to the backside instead of laterally through the array.
why: Array runs ~8-10 C cooler, roughly doubling retention (fact 3) and halving refresh; also widens hammer margins.

title: One metal mask turns the same die into two reliability SKUs
idea: Inverts 'one die design has one reliability spec': a cheap upper-metal mask variant either routes the on-die ECC parity cells into the data path (approximate SKU, +12% capacity, no ECC) or keeps strong ECC with extended refresh (enterprise SKU).
why: The same wafers serve AI-tolerant and exact markets, raising sellable bits ~10% with no front-end process change.

title: Hammer-proof zone of shield-row-separated pages for page tables
idea: Inverts 'every wordline must hold data': one cut mask converts every other wordline in 1/32 of each bank into a grounded shield row; the OS places page tables, kernel code and keys only in this zone, where no row has an active neighbor.
why: Eliminates the highest-impact row-hammer exploits (fact 9) for ~1.5% capacity, letting the rest of the die use cheaper probabilistic mitigation.

title: HBM base-die reroute layer swaps in a spare core die
idea: Inverts 'all stacked dies are essential': one redistribution mask on the base die adds a channel crossbar so a 9-high stack can map out any core die that fails after stacking and route its channels to the spare.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) drops toward ~5%; one RDL mask on a mature-node base die.

title: Charge-trap odometer counts each row's activations
idea: Inverts 'activation counting is digital bookkeeping': the single added mask places a trap-rich dielectric under a tiny gate at each wordline end so every activation injects a small charge; during refresh the odometer's threshold shift is sensed to flag hammered rows, then erased.
why: Exact per-row hammer tracking (fact 9) with no SRAM tables or controller involvement, ~0.3% area.

title: Ferroelectric sanctuary rows hold weak data during idle
idea: Inverts 'volatile data must stay volatile': one mask swaps the capacitor dielectric to HZO in a few rows per bank, forming FeRAM rows on the same sense amps; before self-refresh the controller parks data from mapped weak rows there so the weakest rows need no refresh.
why: Self-refresh rate is set by the 1e-4 rather than the 1e-9 tail (fact 3), ~4x lower idle refresh energy.

title: Thin-film thermometer per mat drives local refresh rates
idea: Inverts 'one temperature sensor per die': the single added mask patterns a TaN thin-film resistor meandering over each mat, read by the periphery to scale each mat's refresh to its own temperature, since mats under hot compute dies differ by 10-20 C.
why: Most mats refresh at their cooler local rate; 30-50% refresh cut in HBM and 3D stacks with thermal gradients (facts 3, 6).

title: Retrofit mature U.S. DUV fabs with one reliability mask
idea: Inverts 'competitive DRAM needs the newest EUV node': a policy-backed program funds mature 2x-nm DUV lines in the U.S. to add one RDL mask exposing every die's internal ECC syndromes and repair ports to a companion controller chiplet, which applies map-based tolerance so cheap, weaker legacy cells serve AI tiers.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4): depreciated, EUV-free tools add supply in ~2 years instead of 5.

title: Merge-mask bridges landing pads into double-charge cells
idea: Inverts 'one cell, one capacitor': one added mask bridges pairs of adjacent storage-node landing pads in a designated region so two pillars act as one ~10 fF capacitor driven by two access transistors in parallel.
why: Creates a robust region (2x signal, ~4x retention, immune to single-pillar defects) for metadata and ECC parity, letting the rest of the die use cheaper, weaker cells.

title: Low-leak isolation switch halves bitlines for weak rows
idea: Inverts 'every row sees the full bitline capacitance': one Vt-adjust implant mask creates a low-leakage isolation transistor mid-bitline; near-half rows are read with the far half cut off, halving Cbl, and the controller maps weak or hot data to those rows.
why: ~2x sense signal and faster tRCD for mapped weak cells (facts 1, 3); extends tiered-latency DRAM into a reliability tier.

title: On-die ReRAM keeps the chip's own weak-cell map
idea: Inverts 'the DRAM die knows nothing about itself': one BEOL mask adds a small ReRAM array in the periphery that stores the die's evolving weak-cell and hammer map, so on-die logic applies erasure decoding and coset encoding at power-up with no external flash or retest.
why: Makes map-based tolerance self-contained and portable across systems; removes minutes of boot-time retention profiling.

title: Slew-limited wordlines reduce hammer coupling per activation
idea: Inverts 'faster wordline edges are always better': one mask adds a high-sheet-resistance poly resistor in each sub-wordline driver path, shaping a slower rise and fall that reduces the capacitive kick and hot-carrier injection each activation delivers to neighbors.
why: Hammer disturbance per ACT cut ~2-4x (fact 9) for ~1 ns of tRAS, with no counters.

title: Contactless RF test coils make every die's retention map cheap
idea: Inverts 'test requires probe needles': one top-metal mask adds an on-die inductive coil and rectifier so whole wafers are powered and read wirelessly in parallel inside a heated chamber for hours of retention mapping without probe cards.
why: Cuts test cost (~10-15% of DRAM cost) and gives every die the full weak-cell map that tolerance schemes need.

title: Thick dielectric collar at the capacitor's leaky top rim
idea: Inverts 'capacitor dielectric must be uniform': one mask defines a thicker, lower-k oxide collar at the pillar top, where field crowding at electrode corners concentrates leakage and early breakdown.
why: Capacitor leakage and breakdown tail cut ~2-5x for <5% Cs loss, shrinking the retention tail and allowing a thinner, higher-k main dielectric.
